finding: The live range of $40-$550 is too low at the bottom and about right at the top. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks; 0.33-1.0 hr in every class): economy 2015 Corolla about $150-$383; midsize 2016 Accord up to about $506 (no aftermarket price found, so no low total; about $276 with the genuine part at a discount price of $236); truck 2023 Tahoe 5.3L up to about $264 (about $95 with the genuine GM sensor at a discount price of $55); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $182-$658. The lowest total we can build is about $95, and that uses a genuine GM sensor at an online discount price plus 20 minutes of labor, less than most shops charge for either; the lowest benchmark is $158 (Jerry). Nothing found supports $40 for a shop replacement: that is roughly the cost of a can of sensor cleaner or a minimum labor charge. A floor near $100-$150 is supportable. The $550 top fits the mainstream vehicles and RepairPal's $274-$381, and is a little low only for a European luxury car with a dealer-list part (about $658 for the 328i). How solid the labor times are: weak. Only the Tahoe has a manufacturer-stated time (GM 1.0 hr), and that operation also replaces the wiring connector, so it overstates the sensor alone. For the Corolla, Accord and 328i no manufacturer time was found; the range rests on a mechanic-written consumer guide's 'book time is usually between 20 and 35 minutes' and a general 'no more than an hour of work' statement, neither vehicle-specific. The job itself is simple on most cars (a connector and two screws on the Accord), which is consistent with the short times. Parts are the bigger variable: list prices found run from $104 (Tahoe) to $498 (328i), and the Accord's two catalog pages at the same seller disagree ($345.55 vs $405.72).
extras: A quote often adds diagnosis (one guide says 0.5-1.0 hr), since a MAF code is frequently caused by a dirty or oiled sensor, an air leak after the sensor, a loose intake tube or a clogged air filter rather than a failed sensor. A shop may clean the sensor first, replace the air filter, repair the wiring connector (one GM bulletin bundles the connector with the sensor at 1.0 hr), and add shop supplies and tax. An estimate is not a quote and not a diagnosis.
